name: Volker Schlöndorff
milestone_by_age_26: Co-directed the highly regarded experimental documentary Méditerranée (1963) with Jean-Daniel Pollet, a film praised by Jean-Luc Godard and included in 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.
early_history_summary: Born to a physician father in Wiesbaden, Schlöndorff moved to Paris in 1956 where he studied political science at the Sorbonne and film at IDHEC, while working as assistant director for Louis Malle, Alain Resnais, and Jean-Pierre Melville on major French New Wave films. He made his first short film in 1960 and co-directed Méditerranée in 1963 at age 24.
family_context_summary: Born to a physician father in Wiesbaden, Germany; his mother was killed in a kitchen fire in 1944 when he was five years old. The family moved to Paris in 1956.
primary_early_advantage_tags: IDHEC film school, Louis Malle mentorship, French New Wave, Paris, Sorbonne
evidence_summary: Schlöndorff's early career was shaped by immersion in the French New Wave ecosystem: formal training at IDHEC, sustained mentorship from Louis Malle (who gave him his first assistant director job), and collaboration with major directors like Resnais and Melville before age 24. His physician father provided enough financial stability for the family to relocate to Paris. The co-directed Méditerranée (1963) gained critical acclaim and appears in 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die. His mother's death when he was five was a formative adversity.
starting_point: Born to a physician father in Wiesbaden, Germany; mother killed in a kitchen fire in 1944; family moved to Paris in 1956 where he studied at the Sorbonne and IDHEC film school.
current_position: Professor of film and literature at the European Graduate School; founding member of the Deutsche Filmakademie; continues to be regarded as a leading figure of New German Cinema.

trajectory.event: Co-directed Méditerranée with Jean-Daniel Pollet, a highly regarded experimental documentary praised by Jean-Luc Godard and included in 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.

Directed Diplomacy, a French war drama selected for the Berlin Film Festival.

name: Håkan Loob
milestone_by_age_26: Set Elitserien single-season records of 42 goals and 76 points in 1982-83 and won the Guldpucken as Swedish player of the year, records that still stand today.
early_history_summary: Born in Slite, Gotland, Loob started playing ice hockey at age five when an artificially frozen rink was constructed near his home. He was a multi-sport athlete in his youth, including being one of Sweden's best table tennis talents, but quit all other sports at age 15 to focus on hockey. He made his senior debut at 15 and joined Färjestad BK in the Elitserien in 1979, winning the Swedish championship in 1981 before his record-breaking 1982-83 season.
family_context_summary: Born in Slite, Gotland, to a family of Estonian descent; his grandparents fled Estonia in a small boat across the Baltic Sea during WWII. An artificially frozen rink was built near his home when he was five, enabling early hockey training.
primary_early_advantage_tags: early hockey start, Färjestad BK, Swedish hockey pipeline, multi-sport talent, Gotland rink
evidence_summary: Loob benefited from early access to an ice rink near his home in Slite, starting hockey at age five and focusing exclusively by fifteen. The Swedish elite hockey pipeline (Färjestad BK, Elitserien) provided a high-level competitive environment from age 19. His Estonian refugee family background is documented but no specific financial or domain advantages are evident. His multi-sport athleticism, including being a top Swedish table tennis talent, suggests natural physical ability that transferred to hockey.
starting_point: Born in Slite, Gotland, Sweden to a family of Estonian descent; grandparents fled Estonia during WWII; started playing hockey at age five when an ice rink was built near his home.
current_position: Head of European Scouting for the Calgary Flames; former president of Hockey Operations for Färjestad BK; inducted into the IIHF Hall of Fame in 1998.

name: Teresa Berganza
milestone_by_age_26: Made her operatic debut as Dorabella in Mozart's Così fan tutte at the Aix-en-Provence Festival in 1957, followed by her La Scala debut the same year and Glyndebourne debut in 1958.
early_history_summary: Born in Madrid, Berganza studied piano and voice at the Madrid Royal Conservatory under Lola Rodríguez Aragón, a pupil of Elisabeth Schumann. She won first prize for singing in 1954 at age 21, made her concert debut in Madrid in 1955, and her operatic debut at Aix-en-Provence in 1957. She had little financial support and worked from a young age to pay for her studies.
family_context_summary: Born in Madrid to Guillermo Berganza, an accountant, and Ascension Vargas; one of three children. She had little financial support and worked from a young age to pay for her conservatory studies.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Madrid Royal Conservatory, Lola Rodríguez Aragón, Aix-en-Provence, La Scala, vocal talent
evidence_summary: Berganza trained at the Madrid Royal Conservatory under Lola Rodríguez Aragón, a pupil of Elisabeth Schumann, providing a direct lineage of elite vocal pedagogy. She won the conservatory's first prize for singing at 21 and had little financial support, working to pay for her studies. Her talent was recognized by the director of the Aix-en-Provence Festival, who booked her for her operatic debut at 24, quickly leading to engagements at La Scala, Glyndebourne, and the Royal Opera House. The post-Spanish Civil War context and financial hardship created urgency in her career pursuit.
starting_point: Born in Madrid to Guillermo Berganza, an accountant, and Ascension Vargas; one of three children with little financial support; worked from a young age to pay for conservatory studies.
current_position: Died on 13 May 2022 at age 89 in San Lorenzo de El Escorial, Spain; final role as professor at the Escuela Superior de Música Reina Sofía; regarded as one of the most admired mezzo-sopranos of the modern era.

name: Jonah Lomu
milestone_by_age_26: Became the youngest ever All Black at 19 years and 45 days when he debuted against France in June 1994, breaking a record held since 1905.
early_history_summary: Born in Pukekohe, Auckland to Tongan immigrant parents, Lomu grew up between rural Tonga and South Auckland. He attended Wesley College where he excelled in athletics and rugby, starring at the 1994 Hong Kong Sevens as an 18-year-old before being selected for the All Blacks at 19. His 1995 Rugby World Cup performance at age 20 made him a global sporting icon.
family_context_summary: Born to Tongan immigrant parents from Haʻapai in Pukekohe, Auckland; grew up in modest circumstances between rural Tonga and South Auckland.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Cousins John Tamanika and Seti Kiole were also rugby players.
primary_early_advantage_tags: extraordinary size and speed, Wesley College, All Blacks pipeline, Tongan immigrant background, 1995 World Cup
evidence_summary: Lomu's extraordinary physical attributes (196cm, 125kg with sprint speed) were apparent from a young age, making him a multi-sport prodigy at Wesley College. The New Zealand rugby pipeline provided the elite institutional pathway that fast-tracked him to the All Blacks at 19. His Tongan immigrant background in modest South Auckland circumstances created both adversity and motivation. The 1995 Rugby World Cup, which coincided with rugby's transition to professionalism, provided a structural wave that amplified his global fame. His cousins John Tamanika and Seti Kiole were also rugby players, suggesting some family athletic lineage.

current_position: Died on 18 November 2015 at age 40 in Auckland, New Zealand; remembered as one of rugby's greatest and most iconic players, the first rugby player to achieve worldwide fame.

name: Nadezhda Chizhova
milestone_by_age_26: Won the European Championships gold medal in shot put in 1966 at age 21, and set her first world record (17.86m) in December 1967.
early_history_summary: Born in Usolye-Sibirskoye, Russian SFSR, Chizhova lost her father at age four and took up shot put at age 16. She moved to Saint Petersburg in 1963 at age 18 to train with Viktor Alekseyev, a leading Soviet coach who had previously trained Olympic champions. She won the European junior title in 1965 and the European senior title in 1966.
family_context_summary: Born in Usolye-Sibirskoye, Russian SFSR; fourth child in the family; lost her father at age four. Moved to Saint Petersburg at 18 to train with elite coach Viktor Alekseyev.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Viktor Alekseyev coaching, Soviet athletics system, Spartak Leningrad, early shot put start, fatherless household
evidence_summary: Chizhova's career was shaped by the Soviet athletics pipeline: she moved to Saint Petersburg at 18 to train with Viktor Alekseyev, who had previously produced Olympic champions Tamara Press, Galina Zybina, and Tamara Tyshkevich. This elite coaching access was the primary accelerator of her career. She lost her father at age four and grew up in modest circumstances in Siberia, creating both adversity and urgency. She took up shot put relatively late at 16 but progressed rapidly under Alekseyev's guidance, winning the European junior title at 20 and the European senior title at 21.
starting_point: Born in Usolye-Sibirskoye, Russian SFSR; fourth child in the family; lost her father at age four; took up shot put at 16 and moved to Saint Petersburg at 18 to train with elite coach Viktor Alekseyev.
current_position: Retired from competition after the 1976 Olympics; worked as an athletics coach in Saint Petersburg. Born 1945, age 80 in 2025.

name: Sunil Gavaskar
milestone_by_age_26: Scored 774 runs in his debut Test series against the West Indies in 1971 at age 21, averaging 154.80 with four centuries, leading India to their first-ever series win in the Caribbean.
early_history_summary: Born in Bombay to a middle-class Marathi family, Gavaskar was named India's Best Schoolboy Cricketer of the Year in 1966 at age 17. His uncle Madhav Mantri was a former Indian Test wicketkeeper. He made his first-class debut for Bombay in 1968-69 and was selected for the Indian team for the 1971 West Indies tour, where his historic debut series made him an instant star.

family_context_summary: Born in Bombay to a middle-class Marathi family; uncle Madhav Mantri was a former Indian Test wicketkeeper who served on Bombay's cricket selection committee.

evidence_summary: Gavaskar grew up in Bombay's cricket-rich environment with the added advantage of an uncle (Madhav Mantri) who was a former Indian Test wicketkeeper and served on Bombay's selection committee. He was named India's Best Schoolboy Cricketer at 17, scoring 246*, 222, and 85 in school cricket. His middle-class family background provided enough stability for focused cricket development. The Bombay cricket system, the dominant Ranji Trophy team of the era, provided a high-level domestic platform. His debut series of 774 runs against the West Indies in 1971 at age 21 remains one of the greatest debut performances in cricket history.

name: Cristina Sánchez
milestone_by_age_26: Became the first woman to complete her alternativa in Europe on 25 May 1996 at Nîmes, France, at age 24, graduating to full matador status.
early_history_summary: Born in Parla, Madrid to a bullfighting family, Sánchez's father Antonio Sánchez was a professional banderillero. She discovered her vocation at age 15 and enrolled in the Escuela Taurina de Madrid in 1989. She debuted with picadores in Valdemorillo on 13 February 1993 at age 20, became the first woman to fight and kill six bulls in succession in a single corrida in Toledo at 21, and was the first novillera to leave through the big door at Las Ventas in 1995.
family_context_summary: Born in Parla, Madrid to a bullfighting family; father Antonio Sánchez was a professional banderillero, providing direct immersion in the taurine world from childhood.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Antonio Sánchez was a professional banderillero, giving Sánchez early and sustained exposure to bullfighting culture, techniques, and networks.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father banderillero, Escuela Taurina de Madrid, Las Ventas, gender barrier-breaking, taurine family
evidence_summary: Sánchez's primary advantage was growing up in a bullfighting family with a father who was a professional banderillero, providing domain immersion from childhood. She enrolled in the Escuela Taurina de Madrid at 17 and progressed rapidly, debuting with picadores at 20. As a woman entering a male-dominated tradition, she faced significant gender barriers that created both adversity and a distinctive platform. Her alternativa at Nîmes in 1996 made her the first woman to complete this ceremony in Europe, a historically significant milestone in bullfighting.
starting_point: Born in Parla, Madrid, Spain to a bullfighting family; father Antonio Sánchez was a professional banderillero; grew up in a taurine environment and discovered her vocation at age 15.
current_position: Retired from professional bullfighting in October 1999; married Portuguese banderillero Alexandre da Silva in 2000. Born 1972, age 53 in 2025.

name: Henri Pescarolo
milestone_by_age_26: Won the European Formula 3 Championship in 1967 with Matra, including victory at the Monaco F3 race, at age 25.
early_history_summary: Born in Montfermeil near Paris to an eminent Parisian doctor, Pescarolo was a medical student when he entered Ford's Operation Jeunesse talent scheme in 1964 at age 22, winning his first ever motor race. He was signed by Matra as a test and F3 driver, and in 1967 won the European F3 Championship, leading to promotion to Formula 2 and then Formula One in 1968.

evidence_summary: Pescarolo's racing career was launched through Ford's Operation Jeunesse, a national talent-spotting scheme that selected him from over 10,000 applicants despite no prior racing experience. His natural aptitude was immediately apparent: he won his first ever motor race. Matra boss Jean-Luc Lagardère signed him, providing access to elite F3 and F2 machinery. His doctor father provided a middle-class safety net and medical career fallback. The French motorsport ecosystem of the 1960s, with Matra's ambitious program, created a structural wave for young French drivers. His F3 championship in 1967 at age 25 led directly to Formula One.
